keyVerseText: And of the sons of Pahathmoab; Adna, and Chelal, Benaiah, Maaseiah, Mattaniah, Bezaleel, and Binnui, and Manasseh.
rootMeaning: The root of עַדְנָא (ʻAdnâʼ) is עָדַן (ʻâdan), which conveys the idea of delight or pleasure, specifically to be soft, pleasant, or to luxuriate. This root suggests a sense of restfulness and enjoyment, going beyond a mere name to imply a state of pleasurable ease or delight. Understanding this root enriches the name עַדְנָא by connecting it to concepts of comfort and satisfaction, rather than viewing it solely as a proper noun.
usageInScripture: The word עַדְנָא appears only twice in Scripture, always as a proper name transliterated as Adna. It refers to two distinct individuals: one from the family of Pahath-moab who returned with Ezra and married a foreign wife, and another a priest descended from Harim during the time of Joiakim. The consistent translation as a proper name highlights its function as an identifier rather than a common noun, yet its root meaning of pleasure remains implicit in the name's background.
theologicalSignificance: The name עַדְנָא, rooted in the concept of delight and rest, reminds believers that God’s people are called to live in the joy and peace that come from Him. Although the word is used as a personal name, its etymology points to the spiritual reality of finding true pleasure and rest in God’s presence. This reflects the Christian hope that through Christ, believers can experience lasting satisfaction beyond worldly struggles. The presence of Adna among those who returned from exile also symbolizes restoration and the renewal of God’s covenant people, grounded in divine delight rather than mere survival.
keyVerseReflection: Ezra 10:30 lists Adna among the sons of Pahathmoab who returned from exile, emphasizing his role within the community seeking restoration. The use of the name Adna here connects the individual to the theme of pleasure or rest, suggesting that even amid the challenges of returning and reforming, God’s people are called to find their delight in Him. This verse highlights how personal names in Scripture carry deeper meanings that enrich our understanding of God’s work in history.
